Hobson, Esq., president Steel Company of Hamilton, Ont.; S. F. Kirkpatrick, M.Sc., professor metallurgy, Queen's University, Kingston, Ont.; J. C. McLennan, Ph.D., F.R.S., professor of physics and director of the physics laboratory, University of Toronto, Toronto; A. S. Mackenzie, Ph.D., D.C.L., president Dal-housie University, Halifax, N.S.; W. C. Murray, M.A., LL.D., president University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan; R. A. Ross, Esq., E.E. (Tor.), M. Can. Soc. C.E., consulting engineer, 80 St. Francois Xavier street, Montreal; R. F. Ruttan, M.A., M.D., Sc.D., professor of chemistry and director of the chemical laboratories, McGill University, Montreal; Arthur Surveyer, B.A.Sc., M. Can. Soc. C.E., consulting engineer, 274 Beaver Hall Hill, Montreal; secretary, J. B. Challies, CE. (Tor.), M. Can. Soc. C.E., superintendent Dominion Water-Power Branch, Ottawa.

By whom were these
gentlemen appointed?

The Governor in Council. I may say that Dr. McLennan, professory of physics in Toronto, is now in England, iand the advisory council have appointed him to represent them on the advisory council there. The advantage which we get, and which they get from that is this: he meets with them and they have information of all that we are doing here along this line, and he gets information from them as to how they are carrying on their work on the other side. It is an interchange of information, of ideas, and of suggestions.

My hon. fyiend, instead of answering my question, gave a long list of handles to Dr. MacCallum. One was that he was a doctor of philosophy, and the other that he was a doctor of science, but in what line of work has he gained distinction? Is it in the line of applied science?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is one of the most distinguished scientific men in Canada. For many years he has been professor of pathology in the University of Toronto. He is a noted physiologist, and also a chemist of high standing. I do not know any better qualified man, from the standpoint of general scientific knowledge, 'in Canada than Professor MacCallum.

I am glad to learn that he has gained distinction in the work of chemistry, because I would suppose that is the most important work that this bureau would have to perform. I recognize the very great importance of it, and all that I was anxious to know was that the work was to be undertaken on practical lines.
Has the hon. minister mentioned any representative of Laval University on that board?

I have not. In preparing the list for the advisory -council the desire Wias to obtain men from the universities, and to make the very best selection of scientific men along practical lines that could possibly be made, and, of course, it must be along scientific lines. Inquiry was made in reference to Laval University, I may inform my hon. friend,

but it was not found that that university had on its list any specially distinguished professor in the lines of work which we require in the advisory council.

I am surprised to hear the hon. gentleman say that, because Laval is affiliated with all the colleges in Quebec. To be told that there was not a man to be found in that university fit to serve on a council like this is news to me.

My hon. friend should not put it that way. A great number of men in Canada are fit to serve on a body like this, but we want only a restricted number, and we try to get those who will best make up that restricted number. I am informed that. Mr. Surveyor is a graduate of Laval.
Is that the lawyer?
Thank Heaven, this is one board that is able to get along without a lawyer.

Laval occupies an unique position in this country. It is the university that first had a Royal charter in Canada; it is representative of one class of the population. In undertaking a work such as my hon. friend is now undertaking, I assume that he desires the co-operation of all the elements of the population. Laval has produced many distinguished men; some of them are to-day in Quebeo colleges-men of high standing. They may be found also in the Royal Society of Canada and in other learned bodies. I am sure that if the minister will give the matter consideration, he will come to the conclusion that it would be good policy to include in this body a representative of Laval University.
At the risk of incurring the unfavourable criticism of the ministeriSir GEORGE FOSTER: Do not be afraid of that.

-I take very much the same position as that taken by the member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles). I cannot help thinking that however meritorious this proposal may be or would be at any other time, this is not an appropriate time or occasion to introduce it. There is the foundation here of a large organisation, involving the expenditure of a large amount of money -money that will be devoted more to organization than to the producing of results. At this time we cannot afford to 6pend money on anything but results'. At a time when the requirements of the

country are so immense, so urgent; when we are descending to the point of soliciting private help from individuals throughout the country for the carrying of our war burdens, we should not enter upon what the member for Moosejaw calls a nebulous scheme of scientific research. My hon. friend mentioned two matters that are of interest particularly to the prairie West. One is the discovery at Moosejaw of a method for the production of gas from straw. This is a matter of inventive genius; it is not in any way indebted to scientific research arrangements; it is not connected with this or any other similar proposal. My hon. friend now proposes to introduce a subsidiary matter in connection with that as an excuse for the establishment of this big organization. If he is desirous of carrying to success the extraction of various articles from the tar product of^ the gas, a small grant to the university of Saskatchewan will produce all the results in that particular that his proposed organization will produce. The same may be said with regard to the tar sand of the Athbaska. If my hon. friend is desirous of securing information that will lead to the utilization of the tar sand, a small grant to the university of Alberta would produce probably better results than would be produced under this organization that he proposes. The time is ill-judged for launching what will turn out to be a very expensive organization, whether it produces any results or not. The amount he asks for is not seriously large; it is the principle that I object to-the principle of introducing new expenditures and new causes for expenditure into the Budget at this time of stress and trial, when we are preaching, or assuming to preach, to the people the necessity of their saving in order that they may serve.

A grant is proposed to be given in reference to the extraction of benzine and toluene from coal gas by means of absorbents for the purpose of accurately determining the quantity of these compounds. There is in the coal gas product in the various cities and towns of this continent a considerable quantity of these two compounds, particularly of the first. These go to waste at the present time; they are valuable, and a solution of the problem would be of incalculable benefit. A grant is to be given to the University of Manitoba under the charge of one of its professors; that is the very thing that my hon. friend thinks we

ought to do. The grant is given under the supervision of the advisory council; it is not a subsidy to assist the university; it is a grant for a specific purpose. The separation of tar from the tar sand is another very important matter. If that problem could be solved, immense benefit would result to the western country. A grant of a small amount, about $1,500, is to be given to that university under the supervision of the proper professor-who is conversant with the question and who is carrying out an investigation at present-to enable him to carry his work to a conclusion. That is the very principle upon which we are proceeding; and that, I think, answers the objection that my hon. friend made in one part of his remarks.

What the minister has said in regard to grants to universities exactly bears out what I say: the practical result to be expected will be reached by the making of small grants to the universities. I am not suggesting that the minister should make grants to universities in respect of these particular questions, but if he feels the impulse to do something, let him make the grants to the universities directly for these purposes; let him not launch upon this country at this time an expensive organization which will cost $91,000 to start-no one knows how much it will cost to carry it on-when all that he proposes actually to spend in regard to the tar sand is $1,500. I presume a similar amount will be expended for research work in regard to the tar extract from the gas from burning straw, and possibly a similar amount as to the extract from coal gas. Those are moderate amounts, and I suppose nobody will object to their expenditure for such purposes. Let the minister make those expenditures if he pleases, and the country will support him, but let him not burden this country with an expenditure of $100,000 for the purpose of giving four or five thousand dollars for actual research work.	#

The expenditure of $100,000 for scientific research in Canada is not objectionable, if we have the proper -organization. It is quite possible, if real practical work is done by the commission, for an expenditure of $100,000 to yield a return of $1,000,000. I suppose one of the best instances of the value to a country of scientific work was that performed by the late Mr. Saunders in the Department of Agriculture. Mr. Saunders developed a seed wheat for Canada which matured some
weeks earlier than any other wheat that had been known prior to this time in Canada.
What wheat is that?

I do not know what the name of the wheat is, but the fact which I have seen stated in government publications is that, through Mr. Saunders' effort, a special wheat was developed which matured very much earlier in Canada than any wheat previously known. I did not know that this fact was ever in question. I could easily put my hand upon written authority in which it is stated by very prominent persons that the result of this was the widening of the wheat belt in western 'Canada by many miles.
I think the wheat to which the hon. member refers is Marquis wheat. The experience of practical farmers has been that it matures eight or ten days earlier than other kinds.

The hon. gentleman may be correct, but I am simply stating to the committee a fact which I have seen stated a score of times. I am giving it to the committee just as I have gained it from my reading, and I have no doubt I am correct in this.
I only wish the statement were true.

It is well known that the work done by Mr. Saunders in this respect resulted in securing for Canada a seed wheat which enables us to harvest wheat very much earlier than we were able to do before, and that was a very important matter in a country in which the summer season is short. If what I have stated is correct, Mr. Saunders' work was worth millions of dollars to Canada.
When the Bill establishing this commission was before the committee, I objected to the personnel of the commission, and I want to repeat my objection. It is not satisfactory to the people of Canada; it is not satisfactory to some of the members of the commission. The men constituting that commission should be much younger men with some practical experience. I do not believe in establishing a commission composed of men who are able to give attention to this work for only a few days in a year. The appointment of such a commission is fraught with great possibilities for this country. The idea is absolutely sound. This is the time above all others in our history when we should be doing work of this kind. The very fact that we have a

tremendous debt to meet in consequence o! the war is one reason why we should engage in this sort of work. My experience-and I am sure it is the case with other hon. gentlemen-is that I am frequently approached by men in my province who are confronted with some problem for the solution of which they desire scientific assistance. They cannot very well purchase this knowledge; they are not in a position to go abroad and bring into this country experts who would solve such problems, and this work should be done by the country, because it will aid in developing our commerce and our trade. Great care should be exercised in the selection of the board. I think a mistake has already been made; in fact, the whole board is a mistake. I do not wish to say anything more about it, because it is not pleasant discussing the personnel of a commission of this kind for, after all, the men on it are distinguished men and amongst our best citizens. But it is possibe to make a very grave mistake in judgment in selecting men for this work even if you do take them from amongst the most distinguished men of our universities. A great problem for a body of this kind would be in connection with soil fertilization. Nothing could be more important than that to this country. If this commission can ascertain some method of providing for the farmers of this country a fertilizer, in sufficient quantities and at a fair price, they will be doing something which will be worth millions of dollars to this country, and the expenditure of $100,000 would be a small matter in accomplishing such a result. What does the minister purpose doing in co-ordinating the work to be done by the commission and that which is now done by other departments? There are scientific men in the Department of Agriculture. There is a vote in the supplementary estimates of $6,000 for forestry studies. I do not know if it is advisable to make an expenditure for that purpose just at present. There are in the Department of Agriculture now some technical officials whose work is particularly talong such lines.
Forestry lines?
Yes.
That' is in the Interior Department.

In the Interior Department to some extent, and in the Department of Agriculture there is at least one gentleman whose work is along that

line. In the Mines Branch there are quite a number of scientific men who devote their time to the scientific side of our mines and minerals, and you will probably find scientific men in other departments. Is the minister going to have them work together or separately? Could not their labours he co-ordinated? Possibly it might be advisable to take the scientific men from all the departments and put them into this branch.

That is exactly what is being very successfully done, and with the greatest good-will on the part of all the departments. They understand each other, and the council works with them and they work with the council. The idea is to co-ordinate and to bring, so to speak, into focus all those different agencies that have been doing excellent work, each by itself. My hon. friend is quite mistaken as to the number of men engaged in forestry work connected with the Department of Agriculture. They are in the Interior De-partmeat and in the Conservation Commission. They are working in strict conjunction, and the experiment, for which this vote is in the estimates to-day, is to be carried out by the experts in the Interior Department. It is not by any means a duplication of energy. The intention is to avoid that and to co-ordinate and concentrate the work upon the development of the resources of Canada.

I understood my hon. - friend from Halifax to say that 6ome of these men are devoting only a portion of their time and energies to this work. If that is so, how many of the council are devoting their whole time and energies to the work? Some of them, surely.

The only one
who is doing that is the administrative chairman. My hon. friend must remember that these gentlemen have been selected because of their eminence and practical knowledge in certain lines of investigation,. It was never contemplated that they should themselves go into the laboratory and conduct experiments. They constitute a committee to set to work, and keep at work, and co-ordinate all the different agencies, and to apply whatever money we may appropriate for work along these lines. All of these men, with the exception of Dr. jVracOallum, are giving their services free, but that does not mean that they are simply taking a holiday and taking no interest in the matter. These men have been at work now foT more than a year, and I know what

they have done. They have devoted a very laTge portion, of their busy lives to this work, and are thoroughly enthusiastic in seeing that it is brought to a successful issue- that it shall not be a mere fad, but give practical results which will be of very great benefit to the country. The council hae met in Ottawa once or twice a month since it was appointed. They sit from three to five days; at one meeting here they sat a whole week. They are not treating this matter as a plaything or anything of that kind.
Their viewpoint was a very good one, and it entirely coincided with mine. A council of that kind, with that desire and that ability to work along these lines, cannot, if good results are to be obtained, all be working separately with no one responsible for the whole work. It wae essential that one man should be appointed to co-ordinate their efforts, and the best man amongst them was chosen-he was their choice ae well as mine-to act in that capacity, to direct, to consult, to keep the whole machine going, as it were, with these men as the motive power. But that is really the smallest thing that has been done. The advisory council has been at work a little over a year now, and in that time has brought together all the different forces in. the Dominion that are engaged in industrial or scientific research, and which hitherto had been doing their work on their own, often duplicating each other, and lacking that energy and spirit that comes from co-ordination with other workers in the same line with a common object in view. The research branch of the Interior and Mining Departments, the Conservation Commission, the Inland Revenue and other research branches, have all been linked up with this general endeavour. In a little over a year all this dispersed effort has been concentrated, and has become inspired witlh a spirit and energy, and with a determined effort to work along these lines, that was foreign to them entirely a year ago. The council has put new spirit into them all.
I do not need to follow up what my hon. friend from Halifax said as to the immense necessity of this work, particularly at this time. A few thousand dollars is a mere bagatelle to the advantage that only one successful solution along some line might bring to the economic strength of this country. This work is almost an absolute necessity, if we are to keep abreast with other nations. My hon. friend says that this is not the commission we should have appointed. I would ask him to give t'he commission a free rein for a while, and after a year or so, I think he will come out of that contemplative area in which he has rested for about a year now, as respects undue criticism, and I think he will then revise his opinion of these men. Nobody can select members to suit everybody; we all have our opinions about them. But I am of the opinion that we have just about the very best council that could have been got together in the whole Dominion.
Would it not be well to have some representative of agriculture on the council?

I suppose there is not a college or university in the whole Dominion which symbolizes agriculture so much as does the university of Saskatchewan, over which Dr. Murray presides. That is the foundation principle of his university, which was founded with a view to the agricultural possibilities and necessities of that great province.

That hardly answers my question. I know Professor Murray very well. He has had very little to do with agriculture in a practical or scientific way in all his experience. He is a very busy man and is engaged in the building up of a new university in a new province. I am not objecting to him being a member of the board at all, because he is an excellent man indeed, one of the very best on the council. Still, I think it would be desirable to appoint another representative of agriculture to the board, with the qualifications I have indicated.

As these scientific men receive no salary, I can see no reason why the minister should not enlarge the council. It is a very big problem these men are undertaking, and there does not seem to be any reason why the number of members should be limited. There is a university in Nova Scotia, St. Francis Xavier, which lias a number of eminent men on its staff who are devoting their time to scientific research, and I am sure some one among them could be found who would be of great value to the council if the minister should make up his mind to enlarge the number, I trust he will not fail to give this proposal his best consideration. I agree with my hon. friend from Halifax that youth counts for a great deal in work of this kind, especially for the chairman, and if the minister has put in charge of this work a man whose best days are over, and who has not the energy required for this work, I think he has made a mistake. I

do not know Professor MacCalhim at all, but I have heard that remark made by men who are interested in the work of this council.
What does my hon. friend think is the age of Dt. MaeCad-lum?
That is what I want to know.
You seem to have assumed that he is an old man. He is a comparatively young man.
What does "comparatively" mean?
He is somewhere around fifty-five or fifty-six. I do not consider a man old at that age.
If that is so, he is almost too young.
The minister should be able to give exact information on that subject.
He may be older than that; I do not know.
The minister has not yet stated the salary to be paid.
$10,000 per year.
Not a bad salary.

Every member of this committee will agree in the principle that it is a proper thing for the Government to pursue research on special problems. It may be very laudable and very profitable for the country to do so. But it may be questioned whether this is the proper time to establish a system of work of this kind, with our finances in the condition they now are and with pressing need for money for other purposes. I think the minister should not ask us to pass the various items included in this vote without giving more details. The first item is for $43,600 for salaries and expenses, including printing, stationery, etc. The minister has told us that the salary of the chairman is $10,000. He has told us, moreover, that none of the members except the chairman receive any salary. That still leaves $33,600, for salaries and expenses, to .be accounted. This Government, since it came into power, has proceeded with almost a riotous abandon to create public officials, and it would look from this vote as though they were going to follow their own bad example. The minister owes it to the committee to

inform it as to how the $33,600 is to be expended. . What is the staff of this bureau to consist of? Do they have to pass the Civil Service Commission and be appointed by that body, or are they to be appointed by the Government of its own motion? The minister has said that Professor MacCal-lum's duty is to keep the whole machine going and that is the smallest part of the work, yet in addition to the salary of the chairman, there is this $33,000. The minister should give more detailed information as to how the money is to be spent.

It seems to me that the criticism which hon. gentlemen opposite are directing towards this vote is founded on a thorough misapprehension of Canada's requirements in the solution of the industrial problems that confront her. Prior to the outbreak of the war it was recognized that Germany and the United States were making more rapid advance industrially than any other nations in the world. Germany was making her advance because she had applied technical education to the education of her workmen, and had solved industrial problems by the application of chemistry and science. Some one has said that if Germany. had been willing to stand by for another fifteen years she would have dominated the world industrially and economically and would never have had1 to fight this war. The United States was making the same advances in the industrial world that Germany was making, and the reason that these two nations were making such tremendous strides was that each had started much later in the industrial activities of the world than England. England had developed her industries along individualistic lines; they were not as all-embracing as those of Germany and the United States. The United States had taken advantage of the co-ordination of wealth -and effort, and had developed tremendous industries. Germany had also attained the same thing with state aid, the result being that these two nations were enabled, through their mighty industries, to take advantage of the intelligence of the world and to apply chemistry and science to industrial problems. England, with her smaller industrial establishments, had been less progressive. We in Canada are just at the beginning of things. Gentlemen on the other side of the House have said that this is not the time to branch out along new lines of work, that we should wait until the war is over, that other things require the expenditure of that money more

than the solution of these industrial problems. It seems to me that these hon. members are entirely wrong, that there never was a time when it was so necessary for Canada to embark on this line of work as it is to-day. Some gentlemen have deprecated the application of science to industry. They must have closed their eyes to what has been going on in the world during the last twenty years. Look what the application of science is doing	in this
war	for the lessening of sickness.
It controls typhoid fever, a disease that, years ago, took two men out of every ten, because in the wars of the past disease took more soldiers than bullets. Look what science has done when applied to industry. We have cheap steel to-day. Why? Because Bessemer applied a process to steel that so cheapened the product that to-day it can toe bought for one-half what it cost a few years ago. Take what has been done in recent years toy the scientific application of electricitj, by making use of our water-powers. To-day munitions are turned out in this country by the use of hardened steel tools in the lathes with a rapidity that a few years ago would have been impossible. We have the steel so tempered and hardened that it can be used in a rapidly moving lathe until the tool practically becomes red hot, so hot that, with the old process, it would have lost it6 point and edge. That is all possible owing to the application of science to industry. Then take the abrasives used in the manufacture of munitions and metal wares. Their production has become possible only through the .application of science to industry. Then if Germany had not solved the problem and were not taking advantage also of Norway's development of electricity in taking the nitrates from the air, the munitions with which Germany is fighting to-day could not be made and peace with victory for the Allies would have come long ago. This line of thought brings another great problem, to our attention. We have in this country great water-powers. We ought to do something to develop another great industry; we ought to take steps along a line of development that will make possible some economic method by which we can get nitrates from the atmosphere, and make a cheap fertilizer for our farmers. I believe that, in the United States to-day, they are spending some millions of dollars in an effort to solve that problem, yet we have done nothing. It seems to me that now is the accepted time
and that we should begin. Reverting to what I said about our having small industries in Canada, and to the point that the great industries of 'Germany and the United States made possible the employment of the best men for the solution of their problems, let me direct attention to the fact that many of the best and brightest men who graduate from1 the universities of this country go to the United States because, when they have graduated from our colleges, there is no opportunity in Canada to secure adequate employment and reasonable remuneration, and if most of our industries have not attained a sufficient size and importance to warrant the expenditure to secure chemists of the highest class, is there any wiser thing for the Government to do than to take the matter in charge, to establish some central bureau or board that would keep in touch with the great problems touching this country's industrial life and the industry of the world, and keep in touch with the brightest minds of the universities, and give assistance to this university or to that, according as its men are working out the solution of one problem or another. I believe that if this scheme is properly managed, it will be of tremendous advantage to the country.. I think it wiser that there should be a central board rather than that grants should be made to this university or that, because if you leave it to the universities-and I speak now as a university man-there will always be a tendency to spend the money on what you might call pure science Tather than on the development of industrial science. If the money that is being expended here should result in the discovery of some process by which the nitrogen contained in the air or feldspar could be made available as a fertilizer, it would do more for this country than ten times or a hundred times the money contained in this vote.
I cannot speak with regard to the personnel of all of the commission. I do not know all the men who compose it. I have for years known Dr. MacCallum, a distinguished graduate and professor of Toronto University; I know Professor Kirkpatrick, professor of metallurgy in Queen's University. I know that he is a man of ability and energy, and that he represents the best thought in the faculty of science of Queen's University. He has applied his brains to the solution of practical problems, and what he has done has been for the advantage of this country. I desire to acknowledge the work that has been done by the young men of the universities. A few years ago an

amount of money was given by this Government to the School of Science at Kingston for the investigation of the cobalt problem, and to see if something could not be done with cobalt ore. Professor Kalmus and his assistants devoted attention to that question for three years, and discovered a process by which cobalt is used as a plating material. It is better and cheaper than silver, it does not tarnish, it lasts longer, stands harder service and wears better. I just quote this simple instance to show how the brains and energy that are to be found within our colleges can be profitably applied. I hope this committee will look' with sympathy upon this vote, and that it will uphold the hands of the minister in trying to get this estimate through the House.
I hope the time is not very far distant when we will have a proposition before this House with reference to technical education. If we are going to develop our scientists in the application of science to industry, we should have technical education so that those who are to be the users of scientific methods may appreciate and make the best use of the scientific processes placed at their disposal.
What does the minister say to my proposal for the enlargement of his board so as to take in a representative of St. Prancois Xavier College?

The principle which was decided upon at the first was that we should not make it representative of all the universities, because otherwise the number would be so great that it would be unworkable. Our people have to come from all parts of the Dominion. I think that I was perfectly right in getting a comparatively small committee. That does not, to a single hair's breadth, operate against the co-operation of every university, scientific institution or scientific person in Canada. It is the object of this
5 p.m. council to organize all the talents and scientific knowledge by way of co-operating committees, and the council is at present developing its scheme in that respect. No person from Laval University down to the college of which my hon. friend speaks, or any other person who has abilities in that direction, will be left unsolicited. All others will be solicited and they will he joined into subsidiary committees working in connection with the central body. That is the line upon which Great Britain is proceeding. She has instituted, under her advisory council, committees in every portion of Great Britain,

each for its special line. The idea is to call out from the country and use in this active co-ordinative work all the ability and talent we have.

Over and above this
advisory council of scientists, there is constituted, I see by the statute, a scientific research subcommittee which is charged with the appointment of this council. How is that subcommittee constituted?

It is composed
of the Ministers of Mines, Interior, Agriculture, Labour, Inland Revenue and Trade and Commerce. With the exception of the Department of Labour, these departments have research branches.

What staff has Dr. Mac-
Calluin surrounded himself with and which will be paid out of this amount of S43,600? How many are there and how are they appointed? Are they appointed by the Civil Service Commission, by the Government or by the doctor himself?

My hon. friend raises a question as to the machinery for carrying out the work and he seems to be seized with a very great fear that there will be some improper manipulation in reference to the help that these gentlemen require. I can assure my hon. friend that there is not the least danger of that. This is not a patronage department in any sense whatever. There will be no patronage in any way. If these gentlemen require to have a question put out in order to get information, we supply Dr. MacCallum with such help as he considers necessary and we apply to the Civil Service Commission for the purpose of getting the help to assist in that work. They are employed while they are able to do the work and no longer. At present there is a secretary without pay, there is a clerk, who has charge of the general department, under Dr. MacCallum, and there 'are temporary helpers to the extent probably of half a dozen who are engaged in the work in connection with these questionnaires. When they finish that work, if other work is necessary to be carried on, they will be at., the disposal of the advisory council, as long as they are required but they will not be kept on a day if there is no work for them to do. I want to assure my hon. friend that it is not the intention with reference to this matter-as indeed it is not the practise with reference to my department-that there shall be any patronage. It is absolutely outside of patronage.
It must be a very important exception.

It must really
surprise my bon. friend from St. John taking into account the way he used to carry on his department.

I think the question is a
very proper one. The minister seems not to have liked it very much.
The hon. gentleman is wrong in that; I want to give all the information.

This is public money and
I presume that any member has a perfect right to ask any question. As long as I am here I am going to do it. The minister's .answer does not satisfy me. He still has $33,600 at his disposal after Dr. Mac-Callum has got his $10,000.
I think it is a very laudable and may be a very profitable scheme in any country, but I doubt whether this is the proper time to embark on such a work, in spite of what the hon. member for Kingston has said. The hon. minister tells us the council has a secretary who is not paid, and there are six or seven temporary employees, and that the expenses of this advisory council cannot be very heavy, because they do not meet often. The only other item of expenditure included in this vote is stationery, and yet he asks us for $33,600. I think he should give us more details, or cut down this item because that sum is not needed for the work he has mentioned.

I will give all the information I can, and the hon. gentleman must not think that I wish to refuse him any. I appreciate his evident anxiety for fear something will go wrong; I could not help but appreciate that anxiety. He said there was $33,600, made up of what items?
Deducting $10,000 salary from the first item of $43,600.
In the first place, these gentlemen who give their services, cannot be of essential service at all unless they meet together.
Do they have regular meetings?	.
Yes.
How often?

Once or twice a month. They have met regularly, not less than once a month and in some months twice. They come from Halifax in the east,
and from points as far west as Saskatchewan. We pay their travelling and living expenses, and they hold about 20 meetings per year. These expenses form a part of the item. Whatever printing and stationery are necessary have to be provided for. If they require printing done, in order to help them out, it will have to be paid for. They will have to provide for distribution of information in different ways. These questionnaires, to which I have referred, deal with the chief work they are engaged in at the present time, and they involve an immense amount of tabulation. I will lay these questionnaires on the Table. When replies to all these questionnaires come in from industrial establishments, colleges, and scientific institutions, they will have to be collated, and the desired information tabulated. This vote will provide for that work. I am not prepared to say whether this $43,600 will be too much or too little. I have made a rough estimate for the first year, because it is experimental, but I can assure my hon. friend and the committee that nothing will be expended unless it is thought necessary, in the opinion of the advisory council.

I have been watching, with some interest, an attempt that has been made to grow trees on Sable Island, for the purpose of keeping the island from wearing away, and becoming more dangerous than it now is. Was that work started under the direction of this board?
That was commenced earlier.
With what success?
I have not followed it.
It might be interesting to direct the attention of the council to that question. The great difficulty is with the soil, which is sandy.

I did not hear the minister mention any special problem to be dealt with, except two in western Canada, one with regard to straw being converted into gas, and the other in connection with sand. Is there any problem to be solved in the other provinces?

The other provinces will not be left out. It is impossible for me to keep pace with all the deliberations of the board, so as to know exactly what they are doing. They are appointed for a certain purpose, and are supposed to be able to select the most important ques-



tions. I remember talking over one problem of great importance which is being considered at the present time, namely, the influence of fogs on sound. That is intimately connected with navigation. There are certain difficulties in respect to it, which, if overcome, will be of great benefit to navigators.

Might I suggest the importance of investigating certain practical questions connected with the fisheries, for example? We have some problems on the coast of the Maritime Provinces, in connection with the fisheries, which have never been solved, and I do not think any attempt has been made to solve them. For example, we are spending a large sum of money in hatcheries, and millions of lobster spawn are scattered on the face of the waters every year. Although we have been carrying on this propagation of lobsters for many years*, no one can say, with authority, whether these lobsters live, develop and grow. It is* a practical question and an expert should be able to solve it with a little consideration. There is another question with regard to the Sipawning place of the haddock and cod. Applications were made to prevent trawling in certain waters-the Gulf of St. Lawrence, for instance-and many fishermen had the idea that that was the spawning place of these fish, which, if so, would be a strong argument in favour of preventing trawlers operating in that locality during the spawning season. I mention this matter so that the minister can direct the attention of those investigators to these problems, which are of such vital importance to the fishing industry.

Does this board initiate the matters which are to be investigated, or will they investigate any subjects referred to them, either by the Government, or by individuals? I should like to know upon what line they proceed. We know there are many questions of practical interest which people would like to have investigated. The question asked by my hon. friend from Kingston, in regard to the production of nitrogen from feldspar is a very important matter, and the problem in connection with that has been very largely solved, but it might be taken hold of in a practical way.
So with regard to the obtaining of oil from shales, which are very numerous in this country; so with regard to obtaining byproducts from bituminous coal. Will any

person interested in work of this kind be encouraged to present his views to the board?

I am quite sure that one of the objects of the board's work will be to find out the problems that are troubling the industrial and productive interests of the country. The questionnaires which have been sent out broadcast have that purpose in view. They are to ascertain from these different -industries and productive interests what their difficulties and problems are; these will be tabulated and work will be begun towards solution of the most important of them through these channels of investigation. Any such questions asked by individuals-not industrial establishments or corporations-will no doubt be taken into consideration by the advisory council. I may say to the member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) that it escaped my recollection that Mr. Surveyer is a professor in Laval University.

I take the responsibility of suggesting, in view of the statements made by the minister and of the other information that we have had here to-day, that the organization which my hon. friend proposes will be a- close corporation for the suppression of individual initiative in regard to scientific research.
I am willing to let it go at that, if my hon. friend is.

In times past considerable sums of money were voted for experiments in connection with the production of peat as a domestic fuel, and electric smelting as applied to the production of steel. I think this expenditure was made under the Department of the Interior.

The Mines
Branch.
Is it proposed that these two matters will come under the jurisdiction and special charge of the industrial bureau which we have been discussing?

The Mines Department is co-ordinated with the advisory committee and they work together. One of the principal aims of the council is to co-ordinate all these different branches of industries. I do not know what practical results have come from these investigations.
I think,that they have succeeded in making a peat which is useful and has been used; how far it has gone towards being a commercial success I do not know. Probably a good deal more money will have to be spent

before the inquiry can be said to be an absolutely successful one.
Steam service between Prince Rupert and Queen Charlotte Islands-further amount required. $5,000.

Is that a
weekly service?

It is a triweekly service. In order to have it carried on under present conditions, the Piost Office Department and the Department of Trade and Commerce had to make a slight addition to the former subsidy.
How many vessels are employed in that service?

One, the Prince John-a very superior vessel.
Department of Finance and Treasury Board- To hereby promote H. Goode to Third Division, subdivision A, $100.

I do object to Parliament being asked by legislation to promote a man from one division to another. If this gentleman is entitled to promotion, he is entitled to it under the Civil Service Act... The House is asked "to hereby promote" this gentleman; what right have we to be asked to promote a man from one division to another? If he is entitled to promotion, let him have it, and let a salary be provided for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend uses language of hyperbole to describe what is really a very simple and proper transaction My hon. friend is spending the powers of his intellect against a young woman, Miss Goode, who is to be promoted from one division to another, to take the position of Miss McConnell, resigned, who was paid $1,200 a year. She is employed in the office of the chief accountant. Miss Goode entered the -service on July 1, 1915, and has passed the Civil Service examinations for stenographers. When she took over Miss McConnell's work it was found that the Civil Service Commission required her to pass in two or three extra subjects not covered in her stenographer's examinations before it would be possible to promote her to Third Division, subdivision A. She is one of the best clerks in the department, and we should have lost her services if we had not been able to promote her. This is not the best time to obtain skilled assistants of the kind in question; we are finding that out in the department. Generally speaking, I agree that it is not advisable in any way to transgress the provisions of the
335*
Civil Service Act;butl call my hon. friend's attention to item 410, in which the Civil Service Commission has been obliged to do this very thing themselves. Item 410 is to provide for the promotion of one clerk from Third Division, subdivision B, to Third Division, subdivision A, $112.50.
They have been encouraged by what the minister has done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So that if the Civil Service Commission, owing to a shortage of help in a time of war, have felt themselves justified in inserting an item of this kind, I do not think that my hon. friend ought to protest so strongly against our promoting this exceedingly efficient clerk to a position in which she will get $900 a year.
Department of Insurance-to provide for three clerkships in Third Division, Subdivision B: one at $800, one at $700, one at $600-$2,100.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Several members of the actuarial staff of the department have enlisted. It is proposed to provide substitutes for those by making appointments in the lower divisions, which appointments it is necessary to create, the department having no vacancies in- this- division. Some of the younger men, who were very desirous of going to the front enlisted.
What has become of the positions which are vacated? Were salaries voted for them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The men who
have enlisted receive their pay and their positions are being held for them, but as the department i3 handicapped by their absence, it is necessary to provide these' substitutes by making appointments in the lower divisions, the idea being that, by the time those men come back, the work will have so increased that it will not be necessary to let any one go. The work of the Insurance Department is very efficiently done, and not with a large staff.
Department of Insurance - contingencies, printing, binding and stationery, including cost of annual reports, further amount required, $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This amount is intended to cover the increased cost of printing and materials, and also to provide for an increased circulation. More and more of the reports issued by the Insurance Department are being asked for each year.
Pensions-compassionate allowance to Private Colin C. McNab for a disability arising from service during the Northwest Rebellion. 1885, $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. member for South Kenfrew (Mr. Graham) is not in his seat. This matter has been discussed at two previous sessions of Parliament. It has been brought to my attention by the Hon. Mr. Graham, by Dr. Maloney of South Kenfrew and some others. Last year, in order that we might have an authentic report upon the case, and be informed as to its merits, I asked the Board of Pensions Commissioners to investigate the matter specially. They did so, and as a result they recommended to me that there was merit in the claim and that an allowance of $1,000 would, in their judgment, fairly meet the case. This item has been inserted accordingly.
Why was the claim refused before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This man, as I recollect the matter, was not a member of the force, but he had been specially requested to go along as an expert telegrapher. It is, of course, very necessary that telegraphers should accompany an expeditionary force. During his employment in that connection, by reason of exposure and the hardship of the campaign, . his health was so affected that he subsequently became totally blind. There are two points: First, as to whether his blindness was directly related to his experience in the Northwest rebellion, and secondly, as to whether it would1 be proper, under any circumstances, to allow him a pension 5s he was not a member of the combatant force. It is open, of course, to Parliament to bring in a special item providing a pension for any person if the circumstances are such as to warrant it. This seems to be a case in which this man's service rendered to his country was a direct cause of his permanent disability through blindness. The Board of Pensions Commissioners have satisfied themselves that the blindness was so related to his experience, and it seems proper, under the circumstances, that Parliament should! be generous to him.
Miscellaneous-Canadian Associated Press,,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The explanation of the vote is: The Canadian Associated Press operates a cable service between Great Britain and Canada. This service was established in 1903, aided by a Dominion Government grant. J. Ross Robertson is president, and J. E. Atkinson, secretary-treasurer. A grant of $8,000 was made last year, when the association requested that such an amount be granted each year 
for five years-this being equivalent to the proportionate yearly value of the five years' subsidy ended June 30, 1915. For its last fiscal year, the cost of operating the association's cable services was $21,188, $13,188 being borne by the newspapers. Thirteen of the largest daily papers in eastern Canada take the direct service of the association, while in western Canada thirty papers get the cables through the Western Associated Press. Through regular news channels, the news so cabled is distributed indirectly to the daily and weekly press of the Dominion. During the past year, 208,-*000 words were cabled in addition to ordinary news of interest in connection with trade and financial matters, questions of interest to Canada and the Empire, etc. Since the war special attention has been paid to the activities of the Canadian forces in England, while a special correspondent pays a periodical visit to the front in France.
Miscellaneous-to provide for the administration of the Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916 ; appointments for the purpose may be made without reference to the provisions of the Civil Service Act, $150,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A similar estimate was adopted by the House last year. It is, of course, only an estimate. The other day I brought down in the House an answer to a question in which I gave the information, if my recollection serves me aright, that the cost of administration for the portion of the year up to March 31 last during which the Act had been under administration, was something under $100,000. We think $150,000 will be an adequate estimate, and it is really a low percentage, having regard to the amount of taxation which we expect to collect from the Business Profits War Tax Act and its amendment this year. The staff was organized last year with representatives in every province, and in some provinces three or four representatives, with such clerical assistance as was necessary to carry out the work.
Do you propose to increase the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It will be the same staff. What I have in mind at present is to extend the business profits war tax staff in order that they may carry out also the administration of the income tax. It will undoubtedly be necessary to have a very large staff to carry out efficiently the income tax measure. It is the first work of that kind that has been done under Do-

minion administration, and every province will have to be covered, but we have a nucleus in the business profits war tax staff, and by expanding that I hope to cover the ground.
Why are you excluding the Civil Service Commission from making these appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not because I do not realize the utility of the Civil Service Commission, but I do not believe it would be possible to get qualified men who were capable of passing the Civil Service examination in time for the organization of a staff such as we have in mind. Take our experience last year. It was necessary to find men of business and accounting experience, and it. is very difficult to get those men. We got men around 35, or 40, or 45 years of age, who had had banking or business experience, and after considerable trouble we managed to get together what I regard as a very creditable staff.
I am quite satisfied, however, that few of them, if any, would be able to pass the Civil Service examination. The type of man you want is a man who knows business pretty well, and men pretty well, and has a certain force of character, but who probably would not be able to pass the academic examination which he might have been able to pass when he was sixteen years of age. My hon. friend from Russell could not begin to pass the Civil Service examination.
I would not attempt it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And as for the leader of the Opposition, he would be hopeless.

Is it the intention of the
minister to appoint members of the outside service in various parts of Canada to administer the Income Tax Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
1 have not given the matter the attention it will receive before we can determine upon the organization. My own view is that if this Act is efficiently administered-and I do not want to administer it unless it is efficiently administered-we must have officials whose business it is to look after income assessments throughout this country. It has been suggested to me that we should use the provincial machinery. I doubt very much the advisability of that. The responsibility for the administration of this Act rests upon the Dominion Government, and I think it must be carried out through officials who are responsible to the Government for administering the Act. I do not think the work should be done by Customs or ether officials throughout the country giving a small portion of their time to it.
I would prefer to have each province organized with an efficient staff whose duties will be to see that assessable incomes in Canada are assessed, and that those who derive them will pay this taxation. If that is not done, I am satisfied that the income tax administration will be more or less a farce. In the cities of this country the municipal income tax is not administered as it should be. Of course, there are a great many exemptions which are not in our Act. Our Act calls for the assessment of the whole income of individuals no matter how derived, and so far as I can see, there are not many loopholes, if any, for escape. I am perfectly satisfied it would be a profound mistake to skimp it, by trying to get men who. will give a little of their time to the work, and who would necessarily discharge their duties in a perfunctory fashion. The Act. should he administered in a business-like way in order that those who are subject to this tax shall pay it. These are but general observations. I am sorry I am not able to answer my Jion. friend more particularly, but he knows how busy I have been during the last two weeks in the House, and I have not yet turned my mind to the question of organization.

If the minister will permit me to make a suggestion, I think he might with profit utilize the services of the municipal clerks and treasurers. In municipalities there are, in all probability, only a comparatively small number of men with incomes liable for assessment under this Act, and it would seem to me to be an unprofitable expenditure to appoint officials of this Government for the special purpose of collecting the income tax when there are not more than a dozen or two incomes to tax in a municipality. The municipal clerks and treasurers are familiar with the circumstances of all persons in the municipality; they are used to looking after the collection of taxes for municipal purposes, and it does seem to me that the collection of the income tax by this Government could be more efficiently done by municipal clerks and treasurers, particularly in the smaller municipalities in Nova Scotia. I would ask the minister to take this suggestion into consideration, and I think upon receiving more information he will conclude that I am right in saying that these men will be

the best persons to perform this work, being able to do it more efficiently and with less expense than officials specially appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am much obliged for my hon. friend's suggestion, which I shall be glad to take into consideration. It was not in my mind, however, that the Government should appoint officials with limited districts, speaking geographically, to look after the administration of the Act. 1 should not like to appoint an official who had only a few assessments to make. But if we had an organization adequate to cover the province of Nova Scotia and other provinces, so that they would all be engaged all the time, I think there could be no objection to such a scheme, and if the information could be obtained, I think that would be the better way. But I am very glad indeed to have the suggestion of my hon. friend.	j

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have made no appointments having regard to political considerations, as nothing could be more unfair than to have polities mixed up with the administration of a taxation. Act. Before making an appointment in Halifax, I consulted a number of the leading business men of the city, and finally a very reputable man, who, I believe, is acceptable to the business community, was selected. I 
think the work there has been carried out quite satisfactorily. In New Brunswick we selected a man who had been for many years an assessor in St. John, and I believe that he has the esteem and confidence of the citizens. The chief collector in Montreal was an accountant who for many years was attached.to the Department of Justice here, a very competent man. Similarly throughout the whole country the appointments have been made, and we have received extraordinarily few complaints with 'regard to the officers administering the Business Profits War Tax.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. D. Stewart in the Chair.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.

speechtext: Loan note exceeding $7,500,000, repayable on demand with Interest payable half yearly at the rate of six per centum (6 %) ; to be used to meet expenditure made or indebtedness incurred in paying interest. on securities of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company; to meet deficit in operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway system and for betterments and the purchase of rolling stock; said loan to be secured by mortgage upon the undertaking of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company containing such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may approve. The disposition of the loan to be subject to the direction of the Governor in Council. The company agree to constitute its board of directors as may be required from time to time by the Governor in Council.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: Is the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) in a -position to give any information in regard to the total -cost of raising the rails on the Grand Trunk Pacific west of Edmonton and generally in regard to the results to traffic and dam-ages to property resulting from the raising of those -rails?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
No; it did not occur to me that the question would arise in connection with this vote although I think it is proper for the hon. gentleman to raise it. The work of raising the -rails is in progress but it is not yet finished.
I am not in a position -to make any statement as to the cost of replacement or the damages, if any, to which my -hon. friend refers.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
Would not the question
of damages to the Grand Trunk Pacific have some bearing on this item? Would there not be a serious and important pay-

ment to the Grand Trunk Pacific because of the taking up of these rails? They surely are entitled to be paid for the rails and they are entitled to payment for the loss accruing. There should be some means of .arriving at the cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: It does not occur to me that it will have any material bearing upon the amount of this estimate because the damages, if any, are quite indefinite and they may he set off for some advantage. It is obviously impossible to make a definite statement as to what the financial consequences would be of the transaction in question, and unless some definite information were had, which cannot well be had at this time, it does not occur to me that it will have a bearing on the question of the amount which Parliament should vote for the purpose of enabling the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate as a going concern during the next year.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: I do not wish to discuss too intimately with the minister that point, but I would think it would have a very important bearing, first, upon the amount of money that would be at the disposal of the company during this current year, and, second, on their facilities for operation. On that point, I am in a position to inform the committee that the difference in the cost of operating is a matter of 250 tons per freight train; that is, the Grand Trunk Pacific can haul five cars of freight less with the road as it is now than it could haul with the road as it was. That is one item that is entitled to consideration. Generally speaking, the transaction is one of such a very remarkable character that I think the country is entitled to a great deal more definite information in regard to it than it has yet received. I cannot conceive of any occasion upon which it would be more appropriate to place that information before the House and the country than during the consideration of this item. Many hundreds of people have been put to great damage, inconvenience and loss, aside altogether from the railway company. Business enterprise in that locality has been seriously impeded. I am prepared to say that not a rail has gone forward to France that has been taken from that track and I am assured that not a rail will go forward to France, first because the shipping facilities are required for food and ammunition, and second, because the rails are not suitable or desired in France, they being very much heavier than are required.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
The information which I have is that 100 miles of rails have
been taken from the Grand Trunk Pacific and that they are either in France or on the ocean and that in the east 30 miles have been taken west of Three Rivers. As to the rails taken up on the National Transcontinental railway, they are all in France.
I may say to my hon. friend, that, while I know that this matter arises in his constituency, I have never been able to understand his attitude towards this taking up of rails. There is no one who is more loyal or has a better appreciation of this war and what it means than my hon. friend. I put to him the question: If an urgent request came from the British Government "We want rails and we want the Dominion Government to give them to us," would my hon. friend give them or would he not? That ,s the position with which we are confronted. Supposing that there is inconvenience, supposing that damage has resulted, does my hon. friend mean to say that this Government should hesitate to take up rails and send them over to France? I do not know whether my hon. friend has been at the front or not. I was at the front and I saw that if there was anything that was needed at the front last fall it was rails in order to get the guns up. What happened at Loos? What happened at other places? They might launch the fire of their artillery and destroy the trenches of the enemy but when they came to follow up they found that no headway could be made because the big guns could not be moved forward quickly enough to destroy the reserve trenches. The Germans might be driven off the first and second line trenches but it was absolutely necessary to move the guns up quickly and to do that they required heavy rails. Light rails were of no use for the purpose. They could bring up supplies of a certain character with light rails but to bring up the heavy guns they needed heavy rails. This is something that I will defend any place in Canada. It needs no defence. When we were informed that the British Government needed heavy rails we said that these rails should go forward and we proceeded to tear them up. The Minister of Railways said he would tear up half the rails in Canada to supply transport for the men at the front; so would I, and I would not hesitate about it. What does it matter about tearing up the rails, if it is going to save the lives of our noble soldiers. The boys at the front are being decimated; they are suffering great hardships, and dying, and, forsooth, because it is going to cause some inconvenience, it is said we should not forward the rails. I have not been able to understand my

hon. friend's position in this matter, because he is a loyal man, and has suffered much in, this -war. He knows the situation at the front, as well as any man in this House, and upon my word, I cannot understand the attitude he takes in regard to the matter of rails.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: I am equally at a loss to understand the position my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Railways have taken. When this matter was up for consideration before, I raised the question as to why these rails were taken from Jasper pass, when rails could have been obtained much nearer the Atlantic coast, and I was told the reason they were taken, from there was because they were of the .same boring as the rails at the front. The minister made the statement that it was necessary to take the Grand Trunk Pacific rails instead of the Canadian Northern rails lying alongside of them, because there was a different boring for the bolts, which, by means of the fishplates, connected the ends of the rails. I say, on the information I have from France, and on the common sense that any ordinary man has, that the reason given is no reason at all. It is nothing more nor less than nonsense, and I think such an argument should not be advanced in the House of Commons by a responsible minister of the Crown. In the first place, these rails were taken from the Jasper pass, 2,500 miles from the Atlantic seaboard, when they had just as good a right to be taken, and could have been taken, from within 200 or 300 miles of the Atlantic seaboard. In the second place, they were taken from the Grand Trunk Pacific in the Jasper pass, when, alongside, was the Canadian Northern, with identically the same weight of rails, the same kind of rails, lying on a road not nearly as well graded as the Grand Trunk Pacific, and with steeper grades. They were taken off the Grand Trunk Pacific, instead of being taken off the Canadian Northern under the pretense-I say pretense-that, because there was half an inch difference in the location of the borings, therefore it was not convenient to use them in France. I say that, in view of such arguments being put before the House, supposedly by a serious Government, I am entitled to call in question the good faith of the Government in this matter, and to say that these Tails were not taken up and sent to France because they were needed in France more than any other rail.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: Why were they taken up?

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: Because it was the policy of t/his Government to wreck the enterprise, and for no other reason. Has the Government ever laid on the table of the House the request of the British Government for these rails? No, they have not.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: Why should they be sent there, if they were not needed?

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: I am at a loss to understand why this Government does certain things. They have accounted for what they have done by talking nonsense.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: My hon. friend should not say it is nonsense.'

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: I am saying it is nonsense, when they say that they had to take Grand Trunk rails, instead of Canadian Northern rails, because there was half an inch difference in the borings.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: That is an important thing;

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: I have information from the front that they link up all kinds of different rails.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: They do.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: And so they can. ' My common sense tells me that for work at the front they do not want 80 pound steel, if they can get 60 pound, or lighter steel. Any man's common sense would tell him that, and when the Government undertakes to tell this House that they took up those rails because they had to, and because it was in the interest of the Allies fighting the battles in France, they are not doing justice to the intelligence of the House or of the country, and when I ask him what the cost is going to be-

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.

speechtext: Certainly, hut the easier the grade, the more economically the freight is handled. After all, with a railroad as with everything else, it is a matter of profit on the work done. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon; we are here for the Government of Canada, but we are here also for the British Empire and trying to win this war. My hon. friend puts forth the argument that this Government, in taking up the rails on the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific, was actuated by a desire to ruin the Grand Trunk Pacific rather than a desire to get forward the rails required by the British Government. Does he suppose that any man in this committee who has a remnant of reason left will accept that argument? Does he think that the people of the country will accept it for a moment? My hon. friend says that without any request from

the British Government, simply in order to destroy the Grand Trunk Pacific, the enterprise of the late Government, we took up these rails and sent them to France. Does my hon. friend think that he is addressing himself to men devoid of reason-because that is what his argument implies. The British Government needed rails to get up the heavy guns. They wanted 80-lb. rails, and they so specified. We sent them 80-lb. rails; in order not to embarrass railways in Canada other than Government railways, we took them in the first instance from the National Transcontinental railway. When we had sent them that kind of rail they wanted us to send the same kind in the further quantities that they were anxious to secure. We then asked Sir Henry Drayton, chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada, to advise us where in Canada that particular kind of rail could be taken up with the least public inconvenience. What else could the Government do? How could the Government have acted more fairly? To what other tribunal should we have applied? The Board of Railway Commissioners is a non-partisan tribunal, responsible not to the Dominion Government, but to this Parliament. On their advice these rails were taken upon the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend knows that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern lines parallel each other in this particular district of which he is speaking; he knows that a composite road was made there. We made the best of the situation in order that we might send forward these rails which were so urgently required and at the same time have due regard to the public interest. My hon. friend speaks of the practicability of joining 60-lb. and 80-lb. rails, or 80-lb. and 40-lb. rails in France. That could be done near the seaboard by the use of hand forged fish plates; there is plenty of time; there is no such inconvenience as there is nearer the front. But when the men have to work under fire, the authorities want rails that can be joined by standard fish plates. That is the reason why, having got 300 miles of rails from the National Transcontinental, they wanted other rails from the Grand Trunk Pacific, of the same weight and the same borings, in order that standard fish plates might be used near the front, where the men work under the greatest possible inconvenience and danger. There it is necessary that these rails should be joined up quickly in order that the great guns may be sent to the front to follow up any advance movement that may be made.

My hon. friend's attitude in this matter is the most extraordinary that I have ever seen taken by any man in this House. He solemnly gets up and puts forward the suggestion that we have not sent these rails over to assist the men at the front, or in response to the urgent request of the British Government instigated by an urgent demand on the part of the eommander in chief at the front. He says: that Is not what you were doing; your sole object was to destroy the Grand Trunk Pacific; you have acted like a lot of mad men in tearing up rails that were not wanted at the front. Without exception, that is the most preposterous statement I have ever heard made in this House. My hon. friend says: that we took up the rails from the Grand Trunk Pacific, and that means that we took away a part of the railway itself which is covered by mortgage in favour of its bondholders, and is a part of the capital investment of the company. I said that this matter had not any bearing upon the item under consideration; I still say that, because the replacement of rails means the replacement of capital. In this estimate we are dealing not with capital, but with the question of deficit on operations and interest upon underlying securities. This estimate is to furnish the Grand Trunk Pacific with $7,500,000, in order, first, to meet the deficit on operation, and, second, to meet the fixed charges for the year. Whatever sum is given the Grand Trunk Pacific in respect of rails taken up will simply be replacement of capital to that extent. As to claims for damages on the part of those who may hold that they have been inconvenienced or damaged by the taking up of the rails, that is a matter for consideration.
I cannot say offhand here to-night how much money is involved one way or the other. In estimating what damage, if any, has been sustained by the Grand Trunk Pacific, there would have to be a consideration as to the value of the rails and the replacement, and, on the other hand, any advantage the railway company might gain as against the disadvantages of which my hon. friend has spoken. I have not passed an opinion upon the matter, and it is not possible for any one to do so offhand. My hon. friend has gone beyond himself in conjuring up fantastic reasons for the action of the Government, which was taken at the urgent request of the British Government in order to meet a very pressing need at the front. He says that we have not placed the papers upon the table. In connection with the war, there are hundreds of papers which we cannot place upon the table of this House, which are of the most secret and confidential character, involving wants and needs of the Imperial Government, disclosing a situation of which they are willing to make this Government aware, but which they would not like to be published to the world. My hon. friend surely would not ask that there should be laid upon the table secret documents that might give to the enemy information of a kind that would be of value to him. My hon. friend, I am sure, would be the last man to suggest that. I cannot help thinking that my hon. friend has been carried away by his partisanship in this matter to such an extent that he feels justified in making these wholly fallacious charges against the Government, which is acting in the utmost good faith in this transaction.
