speechtext:
That is quite satisfactory to me. It is very conclusive on the point.

Of all the arguments that have been put forward on behalf of this very remarkable transaction, the most absurd is that which has just been put forward by the Minister of Finance as the reason why the documents have not been laid upon the Table, namely, because of the special request of the British Government, because of their secret character, because they might give information of value to the enemy. I appeal to the committee if that is not more absurd-if I am not out of order in using the word-than the assertion that it was necessary to take the Grand Trunk Pacific rails because the Transcontinental Tails had already been taken. It is not good enough for this Government, charged with the responsibility of governing the people of this country and protecting their interests, to shelter themselves, first behind the British Government, and secondly behind the Bailway Commission. There is no power nor authority that this Government is entitled to shelter itself behind in regard to matters of administration touching the affairs of the people of Canada. Let there be no mistake on that point. When people are dispossessed of their property, as they have been in my constituency-

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: How many of the hon. member's constituents are affected?

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
I could not say how many, but it does not make any difference if there is only one. His rights are just as sacred as the rights of any other man in any other part of this country, as the rights of any corporation or company in this country. Those people have a right to be protected, and if they have not been protected, if their rights have been thrown aside by the lifting of the rails, then they are entitled to compensation without undue delay. The 'Government, having made up its mind to do as it has done, having the reasons it says it has for its action, has a right to deal promptly and effectively with the people whom it has dispossessed of the value of their property. The enthusiasm of the Minister of Finance for the winning of the war by tearing up the rails out in the Jasper pass reminds me very much of the late Artemus Ward, who, at the time of the American Civil War, declared that he was for the winning of the war even if it cost him all his wife's relations. The minister was willing to tear up the rails out in Jasper pass. There are, however, rails very much nearer the Atlantic coast than the Jasper pass is. Why did ne not tear up a few of them? There are

rails between the good city of Toronto and the town of Sudbury where there are two parallel tracks. Those rails are much nearer the Atlantic coast than is the Jasper pass, but the minister did not touch a rail there. There are three railway lines between Ottawa and the city of Toronto, but none of those rails were raised. I would like to see a little even-handed justice in this matter. If the needs of the war demand that rails shall be taken, why certainly let them be taken, but I do not see why they should all be taken from my constituency to the loss and damage of my constituents, when other people in other parts of the country are left free of any damage, while they shout their patriotism to the four winds of heaven. They can afford to be patriotic if it does not cost them anything, or when it costs only the people out in the prairie West something. That sort of patriotism does not appeal to me, and it certainly will never prevent me from standing up for the interest of my constituents in, this House as long as I have a seat in it. I am willing to stand by the war, by the country, and by patriotism, but I want some of the other men who are doing so much shouting to do a little of the sacrificing also.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext:
In order that the committee may have further information as to this matter, I read this extract from the Order in Council which has been laid on the table of the House:
Further, the minister has had the question ol this further trackage required referred to Sir Henry Drayton, Chief Commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, and he is in receipt of a communication from Sir Henry recommending that a further 300 miles of rails be obtained from the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, partly from that portion of their lines running through the Yellow-head Pass which closely parallels the Canadian Northern, and partly from some of the main line track at other points. The latter to be replaced by other rails.
Then the minister proceeds with his recommendation. There has also been placed on the table of the House a letter from the [DOT]Comptroller of Railways enclosing a report from A. C. Henry of the engineering staff, covering his. investigation ini connection with the taking up of the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway through the Yellow-head pass, in which the comptroller says:
The plan proposed permits of the salving of all the Grand Trunk Pacific rails through the construction of a composite line, made up from the roadbed of the Canadian Northern Railway for 128 miles, and the balance from the Grand Trunk Pacific roadbed, for 77 miles.
After referring to the details of the composite line as shown on the sketch plan at-

tached to the report, which is dated June 12, 1917, he says:
The only disturbance to settlers of any moment is on that part of the Canadian Northern line between Ansell and Leaman, and the reasons for this and the proposed method of dealing with the settlers, is fully set out in Mr. Henry's report.
The work of track lifting is proceeding with the utmost despatch. All section men on both lines and all local labour available, are being utilized, and in addition, we have 150 soldiers from construction battalions, detailed by the Department of Militia and Defence, who arrived at Jasper on the 4th instant.
The first of the rails will be in transit to Three Rivers this week, and unless some unforeseen contingency arises to retard the work, we hope to have all rails in transit by the end of July.
My horn, friend has made the statement that these rails are not in France nor on their way to France. The Comptroller of Railways says he has reports every day as to the position of these rails in their movement towards the front. The statement I have made is absolutely correct. Mr. Henry, the assistant engineer, says in his report:
In my view the general allocation of the composite line, having regard to the fact that rails of Grand Trunk Pacific type are required for shipment overseas, is the only feasible one. Under the proposed arrangement, all the coal mines in operation along both lines are served and the least possible disturbance and inconvenience caused to the settlers tributary to both lines. In addition, there can be no doubt that the single composite line proposed, if properly operated, will be able to handle the traffic of both lines on this section for many years, at a much lower operating expenditure than would be involved in the maintenance and operation of both lines between these points.
These documents are of record, having been laid on the Table. I have no manner of objection to my hon. friend getting up and talking in favour of his constituents; that is an almost universal practice in this House. But I do object to his putting forward in this House the assertion that this Government tore up the rails on the Grand Trunk Pacific, not for the purpose of meeting the request of the British Government or of assisting military operations at the front, but solely with the idea of destroying the Grand Trunk Railway system, which was brought infy existence under the late Government.
'Mr. GRAHAM:	I fully agree with the
hon. member for Edmonton in saying that the reason given as to the fish plates and the borings is not very strong. The fish plates would have gone with the rails that went over; the readjusting of two joints is the only change that would have had to be made. All the switches and branch lines
at the front are not of the heavy weight rail. Any man who has studied railway construction at all knows it is perfectly laughable to make such a fuss about fish plates.
I see in the Grand Trunk Pacific statement that of this $7,494,760.78 only about $2,500,000 is guaranteed by the Dominion Government. I think it is only fair the committee should understand that the amount of money that is being granted to pay the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific is not all on account of bonds guaranteed *by the Dominion Government. Out of the total amount of $7,494,760.78 only about $2,500,000 is under Dominion guarantee.
If I am not mistaken, of this $2,500,000,
[DOT] $1,655,000 is payable on the contract by the Dominion Government on the mountain section seven years from the 1st of January, 1916. So if we deduct that $1,655,000 from the $2,500,000, we would have less 'than $1,000,000 guaranteed by the federal authorities. The balance of this amount is made up of guarantees from the provinces ol Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I notice, too, that there is an estimated operating loss on the steamship company oi $100,000. It had slipped my mind that the steamship company was in this transaction, but it appears that the Grand Trunk Pacific Steamship Company running from Vancouver to Prince Rupert is a part of this agreement, and we have here an amount to assist in making up the operating loss on this line of steamers.
Then there is another very interesting item here-not providing, of course, for interest-namely, that the Grand Trunk Pacific with its branch lines has an operating surplus of $1,100,000. I do not want to make any very lengthy remarks to-night, because I think we discussed this question at great length in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway system, but the entire railway situation in Canada, particularly in the West, is so bound up that that could not be avoided. Thd Grand Trunk Pacific, however, in its present condition can never hope to be made a paying institution, for it is obvious that the object in view in the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific line has not been carried out. I frankly admit that it was a matter of frequent contention between the late Mr. Hays, president of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and myself, that it did not construct a sufficient number of branch lines as it - went along with their main line. Great hopes were entertained of a steamship line between Prince Rupert and the Orient, but those hopes have not materialized, and the

Grand Trunk Pacific system will never be made the great success it was intended to be until that steamship connection is made. I do not wish to detract from the merits of any harbour, but I think there is no better harbour in the world than Prince Rupert, and the optimism of the Grand Trunk Pacific people and the Grand Trunk as well as of the Government was bound up largely in connection with the Orient, from where it was hoped to get through traffic for the Grand Trunk Pacific via Prince Rupert. But so long as we have not got that line of steamships to connect up the Orient with the Grand Trunk Pacific, so long will the Grand Trunk Pacific be merely a local line. At the present time it runs from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert, with no connection of its own at either end. The whole line from Winnipeg east belongs to the Transcontinental.
The haul from Winnipeg east belongs to the Transcontinental, and even the Grand Trunk Pacific has no way of getting to the lakes now over its own connections. It is shut off absolutely at Winnipeg. I have great faith, though, in the future of this line of railway. The Government has handed over to the Senate a Bill providing for the taking over of the Canadian Northern railway and will be in a position, perhaps, to discuss the question of branch lines in a more favourable way than heretofore. There are two or three things needed to make this enterprise a success. In the first place, I believe that steamship connection with the East is absolutely necessary, because one of the great objects of the line will be unattainable if we do not have that steamship line. In the second place, I am inclined to think provision must be made for the construction of a greater number of branch lines, particularly in the prairie country and perhaps in some of the valleys of the mountains. As to the Grand Trunk Pacific running a line to Vancouver, there is now a line projected and partially constructed over which there has been a great deal of difficulty, and I would not dare discuss that. But with the Canadian Northern railway in the position it will be now, in the hands of the Government, perhaps some of this difficulty might be obviated. The great object of the Grand Trunk Pacific was to get a through fine via Prince Rupert to the Orient. A question was raised by the Prime Minister the other night about the co-operative administration of roads. If he meant that all the fines are to be under one ownership, it would be a big question to discuss. My 
own view is that there are a thousand and one things to be considered in addition to rates, and that without competition you would lose a great deal of the benefit, or rather you would fail to derive benefit that you would have with competition. Take, for example, car distribution. While we have an Act dealing with this subject and many regulations covering it, the fact remains that laws and regulations do not operate as advantageously as competition. A shipper between here and Toronto informed me that now that he has three fines of railway passing his town he has no difficulty in getting a car at any time. His shipping with competition is much more advantageous than with one fine. The Board of Railway Commissioners would say: You must have a car at a certain time and the rate must be fixed at a certain amount, but the little details that competition brings do not come to the users of a line without competition. I believe that some method could be devised by which we could arrange for the use of fines by roads other than the owners of those lines in a better way than we have been able to do heretofore. The Canadian Pacific Railway is very much crowded in certain parts of the West, and has been discussing double tracking a large mileage. It has already expended many millions of dollars for this purpose. I see no reason why provision could not be made to relieve the congestion on any one line by operating part of its traffic over another parallel fine on which the traffic was not so heavy, so that the business of the people would not be retarded, because the people of the country have built these roads to a 9 p.m. very large extent. The Prime [DOT] Minister spoke about co-operative management. I think it would not need co-operative management exactly, but certain terms could be laid down under which one road would use the rails of another and a car could be handed over by one company to another on definite terms laid down by the commissioner. In this way two parallel roads could be used as a double track system with great benefit to the people.
As to the future, I have confidence that the railway mileage of Canada is not too great. It may be too great for the production of Canada at the present time, but not for the productiveness of Canada, and it will be for the people and Parliament of Canada to see that, when the war is over, we have the people to develop all our western country; and this railway mileage will

not be excessive for the productiveness of our country when we have people on the land, for with the productiveness of the land will come the productiveness of all our industries, because, after all, our future is bound up not in any one thing but in many things. I received information to-day about a mining proposition that seems to have very great prospects. I was asked if it would be possible to get the Government to build a branch line to a certain mining development. My advice was that the Government would probably be from Missouri just now and would have to be shown before extending mileage, but if in any part of Canada there was a development for the good of Canada, Parliament would be ready to vote money for any reasonable proposition of that kind if it were a paying one.
So far as the Dominion is concerned, we are not paying this money so much for securities guaranteed by the Government as to aid the projects of other guarantors of the securities, and in this connection I may be pardoned for saying that I have always had a rather kindly feeling for the old Grand Trunk as one of the pioneer railways of Canada. The Grand Trunk is committed to the Grand Trunk Pacific very heavily in guarantees, and I believe that the Govern,-ment at the present time could not do else but take such step as this unless we are going to embarrass the Grand Trunk and place it in a position which I still maintain we should not allow our roads to get into at the present time, as our own credit is bound up with theirs to a larger degree than some people seem to realize or admit. While I realize the financial situation, I am not pessimistic at all as to the future of Canada and its railway projects. I believe that in years to come, when the great development of our country is to take place after the war and we have to face all these situations, the people of Canada will be capable of facing all these difficulties. We all believe that the resourcefulness of Canada is equal to any demands that may be made upon her.
It will not be long, I hope, before peace will come and we will have an opportunity of arranging our financial affairs so that we can proceed with the development of the country, which for the time being has been retarded, but which has only been checked and not stopped. The way in which they have acquitted themselves has shown the people of the world that the men produced on this half of the North American continent are worthy of their sires, and what they
have accomplished and will still accomplish in their fight for freedom is indicative of what they can'do when peace comes in the development of their own country.
Item passed.

Mr. G-RAHAM: Does the minister think that at this time it would be inflicting any great hardship on our artists if we did not have this vote? speechtext: I wrs influenced by the same view that has moved my hon. friend to express himself as he has. I think his criticism would be amply justified if we had maintained the original vote. This country has -been in the habit of voting $100,000 a year to encourage Canadian art. This is not for the purpose solely of giving Canadian artists work. This National gallery lends pictures to all Ithe cities throughout Canada, especially, I understand, in the West, so that the work is really a national work. The vote for the year preceding the war was $100,000, last year it was cut down to $25,000, and this year the amount placed in the estimates was $8,000, but it was thought it would have a serious effect on the artists and sculptors, and it was decided to place an [additional $10,000 in the estimates, which will make the total vote this year $18,000. I do not like to ask Parliament to spend money for anything other than practical purposes, especially during the war, but I feel a certain kindness towards men engaged in art and science. They do more for the nation than we realize, and I think we should be generous, rather than otherwise, with them. This is not a large amount. It is the amount barely necessary to take care of commissions which have already been given, and it will not have any appreciable effect on military efforts during the war. The money is paid out to artists. Some meritorious cases have been brought to my attention since the war broke out. We have some notable sculptors in this country, men who have brought credit to Canada by their work. Some of them have devoted their lives to the profession, and the war has caused a -stoppage of orders. We have been gradually slowing down in the matter of this vote, hut we think we have given fair consideration to these artists and sculptors.

It is quite true that the amount is insignificant, -and hardly worth while talking about, 'but there seems to be a principle underlying it, and if the minister by governmental action is going to take care of all the individuals in Canada who have -suffered by the war he will require a Large appropriation. Our pension bill is going to be very heavy, and there is a continuous cry-and I think a proper cry- that more should be done for the returned soldier, for those who are entitled to pensions, for everybody who has suffered through the war. I wish to- refer to a case

in my own' constituency, and I am sorry the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames), who is head of the Patriotic Fund is not here. I refer to the case of a woman whose husband was killed or disabled at the front. She did not apply for separation allowance until just lately, and the Patriotic Fund authorities of the province refused to give her any separation allowance, because she did not apply in time, and they claim they are hard up for money. Every fund that is being distributed for the benefit of the soldi ns is short of money at the present time. The principle I object to in this item is the specific favour to some people who cannot show that they deserve anything at the hands of the country, except for a sentimental reason. Are these artists fighting at the front? Are they of the proper age to go and fight? Who are they? I can conceive that there are some young budding artists who have gone to the front and are fighting, and I would not object to paying those men. The Kaiser sent artists to the battlefields to portray the valour of his troops. But when a widow is refused separation allowance from the Patriotic Fund, because, forsooth, she did not apply in time, it is coming to a pretty pass. She could not even get the back pay of her husband. I do not believe we should be extravagant in our allowances, unless it is advisable in the national interest. These artists are doing good1 work in the. development of art, and elevating the public mind to a higher plane, but just now I would say that we should not vote this money.

subtopic: LOAN OP $7,500,000 TO THE GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC.
speechtext: I desire to endorse the sentiments of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy). Not long ago we had the argument that, if the income tax were passed, the rich man would not give to the Patriotic Fund. I have one case in mind in regard to which I had correspondence with the authorities in regard to a separation allowance. The authorities did not know that tney could make tfie allowance, and so forth. It appears to me that, as far as it is possible, the Government should just pare down to the very bones the financial necessities of this country. I have some regard for artists and sculptors and so on, but when we get down to the real necessities, why should1 artists and sculptors have to be taken care of more than men who, by reason of the war perhaps, have suffered just as much as they have? These men have as much right to be considered, but not on the lines of aestheticism, as suggested by the Minister of Finance. Why should the artist be taken care of any more than other men who have suffered? We know that there are thousands of cases of men and women, who, by reason of this war, have been deprived of a livelihood, and many women have not only been deprived of a livelihood, hut have suffered a great hardship by the loss of relatives and helpmeets. After all, when we go out and talk to the people and say, "Now, we must have thrift here, and production there, the country is in this state, and in that state, and the very worst is liable to happen to us," I do not know why the artists should get a grant of $18,000 out of the hard earned money of the people. These times, when we are talking of hundreds of millions of dollars $18,000 may not look large, but every little helps, and, so far as I am concerned, I cannot see that this vote is necessary. .These men have taken up this line; perhaps I am not inclined to regard it as poetically as the Minister of Finance, but the artists and sculptors have chosen their profession the same as you or I chose our professions, whether it be law or medicine or anything else. If these artists are deprived of their livelihood, they are in no worse position than thousands of other men in the country, and I do not know why the taxpayers of the country should go down in their pockets to recoup them. It appears to me the item should be struck out.

This vote of $5,000 is to cover the cost of the sinking of an artesian well, providing boiler and pumping engine, making use of the large tank which at present contains salt water, which would be emptied, and pumping the fresh water into this tank. This water would then be distributed through the present fire mains and branches laid to each building. The estimated cost is as follows: Sinking well, $2,000; boiler, pumping engine and shelter for same, $1,650; laying branches from main to the different buildings, with valves, excavations, etc., $463; incidentals and contingencies, say, $887; total, $5,000.

No.
Will you ask for tenders?
It may be hard to get tenderers. If so, we can do the work ourselves.

There will be no trouble in getting people to do the work. Will the minister ask for tenders? On a 
public work costing over $5,000 I think the minister is expected to call for tenders.

This vote cannot be absolutely necessary, because the money- was voted last year and nothing was spent. Take for instance, this item of $123,000 for Gross Isle quarantine station, which has already cost a large amount of money. This amount was voted last year, so apparently there is no urgency, because not a dollar oi money was spent. We must get ready for the immigration that will come immediately after the war. If we have this vote passed, we

shall be in a position to proceed with the work as soon the war looks to be ending.
Mr. A. K. M1ACLEAN: You could not commence until next spring, anyway.

But we can call for tenders. Without a vote, it would be impossible to proceed with this building if the war should cease. We expect immigration after the war, and the Minister of Agriculture claims that this building will be absolutely necessary then.
Will the war end before next spring?
We thought so last year when this vote was taken.
On what grounds did my hon. friend think so?

I had my own views, and I think they were shared by a great many other people. To-day some people think the war will last one or two years more, and others think it will be over in the next six months.
What does the minister think?
I hope it will. At all events, it is better to have this vote passed in case it does, so that we shall be prepared to go on with the work.
Does the minister think that the immigrants will swim across the Atlantic or come over by aeroplane?
They may come both ways.
That is the only way they can come immediately after the war.
I do not say that.

There will be very great demand upon transportation facilities to bring our soldiers back to Canada after the war. I do not like the minister to put forward to the House, or that we should approve of the idea, that immediately upon the war being over the Government will rush into all kinds of expenditure like this. As my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) suggests, it must be quite a time after the war before any immigrants will be able to be transported across the Atlantic. It will take two years at least to get our soldiers back to Canada.

It would take at least a year to complete this building after work on it was commenced, and by that time surely
our soldiers would have been returned. We want to be ready when immigration comes.

Would it be at all possible that this vote was put on this year and put off last year because the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) knew there was not going to be an election last year, and that there is probably going to be one this year? That would not be within the realm of probability, I suppose?
I would not do that.
That supposition would not apply to the rest of these items that were in last year, and are now being revoted.
We struck out all the election ones.

Perhaps I am responsible-for most of these items being here and' being pressed. We have been under very serious disability at Grosse Isle. The last time we had much disease there, we had to get tents, because there was absolutely no hospital accommodation. If, after this war, as usually happens after big wars, there should be much typhus or other bad disease, we should be ' in a most deplorable condition at Grosse Isle.
We have the foundation of a hospital there, and it is a matter of urgency that the buliding should be completed. I have been earnestly pressing this on my colleagues for the past three years. I can assure my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Pardee) that there is no politics in this particular vote.
Perish the thought!

The main estimates for Public Works amount to $16,000,000. That would be a large expenditure even in. peace times. Now it is proposed to add nearly $3,000,000, making about $19,000,000 to be voted for Public Works this coming year. The minister would be well advised if he would endeavour to make a reduction, as this is quite without justification.
The estimates last year were $30,000,000, so there has been a reduction of over $10,000,000. These items are very urgently needed; most of them are small items for repairs that we could not avoid.

The supplementary estimates total $50,000,000, which is away beyond any thing any Government has ever asked. The minister cannct justify the ex-

travagance in his department by comparing this year's estimate with last year's, because the estimate of last year was beyond all reason. two and one-half times what they were in the last three years of my administration. The Government went wild over public works, and their extravagance was beyond anything in the history of any country. Now, when the war is on, it is proposed to spend in one year more than one-half of the amount expended in the last three years of Liberal administration during times of peace, when the country was prosperous, when population was increasing, and additional public works were necessary. lit is startling that the minister should ask for such a large amount of money.

While it is true that in the first three years of this Administration the [DOT] Public Works estimates did increase very much, it must be remembered that the Government undertook the development of all the large harbours, Victoria, Vancouver, St. John, Quebec, Halifax.

Many of these works
had been undertaken, and the work at Halifax is, I think, altogether chargeable to the Railways and Canals Department, so that is in addition to this enormous expenditure.

Even leaving Halifax out,
there have been very large expenditures under the Public Works Department for harbour improvements. The expenditure in the last year of the hon. member's administration was $14,338,000.

In 1915-16 it was $16,150,000. Then there are all these large works for which the contracts have been let and which must be carried out. We are decreasing this year.

We are decreasing the estimates by $10,000,000 in the Public Works Department, so although we expended $16,000,000 last year, it will be less this year.

[Mr. Pugsley.l

I think these items might be abandoned for this yeaT. I doubt very much that in any case the expenditures will be made. Then, for my own province of Nova Scotia,

Therefore, I agree quite heartily with the remarks made by the hon. member for St. John. It appears1 unfortunate to ask Parliament to vote these sums at this time. A few months ago, the late Minister of Public Works, in a speech at Montreal, said that he was cutting down the public works expenditures to about $7,000,000 and was eliminating everything. I suppose recommendations were made by members.

No.
Kingston Royal Military College-enlargement of educational block, $150,000-to complete new dormitory by adding two wings, $100,000.

This vote of $150,000 is asked
to make provision towards the extension of the educational block of the Kingston Royal Military College. In their notes on military buildings, dated 14th October, 1912, the Militia and Defence Department stated that in view of the increased number of cadets who are accommodated at the college it is found that the present educational building does not provide ample class-rooms, dining-rooms, recreation rooms, etc., and it is proposed to extend the present build-to this end. The actual accommodation required consists of mess-room, 75x40, for 300 cadets; library; one big lecture hall, which will hold all the cadetsi at a time for general lectures, etc.; a draughting room; two' additional lecture rooms for classes of 50 cadets; and a chemical laboratory for practical work. The present mess, draughting and book Tooms in the old building would be used for other purposes. In a reply to a letter from the Deputy Minister of Public Works of 7th June inquiring as to the necessity of a list of works requested by the Department of Militia and Defence to be noted in the supplementary estimates, the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, under date 23rd June, states as follows:
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of-the 7th instant, and to inform you that the various items contained in your letter have been carefully gone into, and it is requested that the following items which are urgently required be provided for In your supplementary estimates :	Knlargement of educational block, $150,000 ; complete new dormitory, adding two wings, $100,000, It is hoped that every effort will be made to provide these items This extension of the educational block was recommended by the Militia and Defence Department, December,'1913, October 31, 1914, and October 24, 1916.
Is it not a fact that applications for admission to this institution had to be refused this year for lack of accommodation?
That is true.

These are big items, and if they were for something else, I would be inclined to oppose them; but the Royal Military College has proved itself such a wonderful institution, and its graduates have shown themselves to be such brave and splendidly equipped men during the present war, that I would hesitate to object to any vote for the improvement of this great college. Even in peace time the education given at the Royal Military College has been such that some of our leading men have been produced by that institution. The training is not, as some people appear to think, only physical, but there is a mental training, and a course of study to equip young men for the activities of life in a practical way, which might well be envied by some other institutions. If those in charge of the Royal Military College assure the Government and Parliament, as I believe they do, that this vote is necessary for the better equipment of this institution, and, as I am privately informed, for the present needs, I would be in favour of passing these items. If it be true, as we have been told it is, that on account of lack of accommodation, applications have been refused this year to young men who wish to enter the Royal Military College, then we cannot too quickly remedy that defect.

The original educational building is the building now being used for the education of cadets. The cadets are intensely crowded in that building. I think the original scheme of accommodation was for some 80 pupils. Now they have a great many more there, and the demand on the part of young men to enter the college is so great that we have competitive examinations. The second item is to complete the new dormitory by adding two wings. Some five or six years ago, before the dormitory building was erected, one part of it was bricked up. The main building is stone, and, the idea is to remove this brick, and to complete the building by the erection of the additional wing. The commandant tells me it is absolutely essential, if good work is to be done, that further dormitory and educational accommodation must be provided, and those who have followed the history of this war must be aware' that a great many of the men who received their training at that institution

have by their conduct won distinction for themselves and for this country.

British Columbia public buildings-William's Head quarantine station water supply, $150,000.

This is a large item.
What is the explanation?

This amount of $150,000 is
required to provide an adequate water supply for the quarantine station at William's Head. The'present water .supply is obtained from the Quarantine lake, a distance of 3% miles, .and was installed about 1894. It was repaired on many occasions between 1900 and 1913; but constant attention is necessary in stopping leaks, etc. In case of fire the pressure would be greatly inade-[DOT]quate and the chief of the fire department

states that the existing conditions are extremely dangerous and unsatisfactory. During the summer months the watershed from which the present water supply is obtained dries up, and there is always a scarcity of water. To overcome this serious drawback it is proposed /to obtain a new source of supply. The proposed work consists in the construction of a water main from a point known as. " Bray's Farm " on the waterworks system of the city of Victoria, to the quarantine station at William's Head, a distance of about 8| miles. The construction of this main is. in accordance with an offer made by a resolution of the municipal council of the city of Victoria on the 28th May, 1917, as follows:
Resolved, that the Water Commissioner be authorized to submit an offer to the proper official of the Dominion Government to supply water from the city water works to the said quarantine station in accordance with arrangements to be mutually agreed upon, embracing the following general terms and conditions, namely, to sell water to the Dominion Government for this purpose, delivered at a point known as "Braye Farm," at six cents per thousand gallons, the Government to furnish and lay the necessary main, and the city to maintain said main, after it is laid, for a period of five years.
In view of the increasing prices for cast iron pipe it is proposed to use the pneumatic tubes which have been in storage in Toronto for post office purposes and thereby effect a material reduction in the cost of the work. The chief architect of the Department of Public Works in a report dated 23rd June, 1917, states as follows:
Since negotiations with regard to this supply have been in progress the cost of cast iron pipe has advanced very materially. In January, 1917, our resident architect at Victoria estimated the cost of 10-inch water pipe on that date as $52 per ton. I am now in receipt of an estimate from him, dated 22nd June, in which the price is quoted at $85.20 per ton. This difference in cost of cast iron pipe will, of course, very materially affect the estimate for the cost of the work, which was about $150,000.
I have taken up the matter of using the pneumatic tubes which we have in storage in Toronto, with Mr. Chipman, C.E., of Toronto, and have received from him a report as follows:
That from the tests made on the pneumatic tubes he is of the opinion that the pipe would prove satisfactory for water, works purposes under a working head not exceeding 300 ft., but before being used they should be thoroughly cleaned, re-coated, tested and weighed; and that greater care will be necessary in laying these pipes than in laying standard cast iron water pipes. The pipes must be laid more closely to grade and to line than with standard pipes. For a long conduit these pipes would be equivalent if not superior to the standard pattern of pipes. He states he would have no hesitation in using these pipes on a water works system provided they were cleaned, coated and tested.

I know there was a very large number last year. .

The Orient.

Dawson post office-vault, $10,000.

Some days ago I put some questions on the Order Paper with reference to this item. I asked the minister if he had any report from his officials asking that this expenditure be made, and he answered yes. I also asked him to produce the correspondence, and he replied in the affirmative, but I have not received it yet.

I remember looking up the matter. All who have made recommendations in this matter agree that the vault is in a very bad condition. The deputy minister will send over the correspondence to my hon. friend. I understand that a telegram came not very long ago from Ernest Revard saying that this expenditure was no longer necessary, but that was when he was no longer agent of the Public Works Department. He seems to have changed his mind since he severed his connection with the department.

There is a vault there at present, is there not?
'Mr. REID: This vote of ?10,000 is to be applied in tearing down and rebuilding the vault in the Dawson post office building, which has been sinking. This vault was not built on a proper foundation in the first place and is gradually dropping down into the earth and at the same time toppling oveT; in its present condition it is not fireproof, and in the event of the building being destroyed by fire, the vault would he almost certain to topple over and break up, and even if it stood, would not protect the contents from fire.
Dawson being built on a glacial formation, any building or heavy weight, to be substantially placed and remain true in its position, must have foundations put down (12 feet) through the muck and ice over burden to the frozen gravel below. Nothing else will stand. The weight of this vault, as it settles, is shoving over the whole post
office building to such an extent that doors and windows have been crushed out of posi-tiorf, the floors and ceilings cracked and pulled down to a slant. The present vault is enclosed in the main building, and it is proposed to erect the new vault outside of and connecting with the building on the inside only. The vault doors will be stationed, and access will be had to them from the main building. The outside dimensions of vault will 'be 12x14 feet, with stone wall 12 feet high; brick wall on top 25 feet high, and chimney erected at the corner of the vault. The reconstruction of vault has been reoommended by the Department of the Interior October 20, 1916, and by Mr. George Black, Commissioner of the Yukon Territory, in a letter dated 24th August, 1916. I also remember seeing a letter from the Collector of Customs, another from the postmaster, and one from Mr. Revard himself.

Does not the minister think it would be well to have an inquiry to verify the facts, inasmuch as Mr. Revard has notified- the department that .there is no expenditure required, as the vault is in good condition? Does not the minister think it would be well to inquire why Mr. Revard has changed his mind?

I feel this way about it. Mr. Revard, when agent of the department recommended this expenditure. It hak also been recommended by the gentlemen I have mentioned, in all of whom I have confidence. I think that Mr. Revard must have some grievance, and is now trying ito prevent this expenditure. At -al) events, the agent of the department will look into this matter before we proceed with it.
Who is the agent?

No one has been appointed
yet.
When did Mr. Revard cease to be the agent?

I do not know the exact
date, but the correspondence will show.
Would the minister let the item stand for the present?

I had the privilege of'
being in Dawson city a year ago last summer, and was taken through this building by the officials. It was undoubtedly in a very dangerous condition. The floor had sunk very considerably, and the partitions had drawn away from the ceiling. It was impressed upon me how necessary it was to have this vault rebuilt. I know nothing

whatever as to the expenditure, but most assuredly the building was in a very dangerous condition,
Item stands.
